tests.name: Conduct Search Engine Reconnaissance for Information Leakage

reporting.What: Uses search engines and third-party indexing services to find sensitive design, configuration, or internal information about the application or organization that has been exposed publicly.
reporting.Why: Leaked data such as credentials, internal paths, or architecture details gives attackers a head start and can be found without ever touching the target directly.

reporting.What: Determines the type and version of the web server through banners, response headers, and behavioral differences.
reporting.Why: Knowing the exact server and version lets an attacker look up and target known vulnerabilities, so exposed version details increase risk.

tests.name: Review Webserver Metafiles for Information Leakage

reporting.What: Analyzes metadata files such as robots.txt, sitemap.xml, and security.txt to uncover hidden paths, functionality, and other details about the system.
reporting.Why: These files often list sensitive or unlinked locations that were meant to be hidden, which effectively hands attackers a map of areas worth probing.

reporting.What: Enumerates all in-scope web applications, domains, subdomains, and virtual hosts using passive and active DNS techniques and certificate transparency logs.
reporting.Why: Forgotten or unmanaged hosts are frequently the weakest entry points, and you cannot secure or test assets you have not discovered.

tests.name: Review Web Page Content for Information Leakage

reporting.What: Reviews page comments, metadata, redirect bodies, JavaScript files, and source maps for sensitive information or debug artifacts.
reporting.Why: Developers often leave secrets, internal endpoints, or logic hints in client-delivered code, and source maps can expose the original source in full.

reporting.What: Analyzes requests and responses to catalog every place the application accepts input, including parameters, headers, and cookies.
reporting.Why: Every input is a potential injection point, so a complete list is required to test the application thoroughly.

reporting.What: Maps the application's principal workflows and the paths a user can take through it.
reporting.Why: Understanding intended flows makes it possible to spot where they can be skipped, reordered, or abused, and ensures testing coverage.

reporting.What: Identifies the frameworks and components used by the web application through headers, cookies, file structures, and page markup.
reporting.Why: Knowing the framework reveals known vulnerabilities, default files, and common misconfigurations that can be targeted.

reporting.What: Identifies the specific off-the-shelf application or CMS in use (for example, a particular wiki, blog, or e-commerce platform) and its version.
reporting.Why: Popular applications have publicly documented exploits and default settings, so identifying one quickly narrows down likely weaknesses.

reporting.What: Documents the architecture of the application and the technologies in use, such as proxies, load balancers, databases, and third-party services.
reporting.Why: Each layer can introduce its own weaknesses and trust boundaries, and an accurate picture guides where to focus deeper testing.

reporting.What: Reviews network-level configuration of the systems supporting the application, including frameworks, default settings, and cloud or container isolation controls like security groups and network policies.
reporting.Why: Unpatched software, default credentials, or overly permissive network rules can expose the application regardless of how secure its own code is.

reporting.What: Checks that default and sample files are removed, debug features are disabled, logging is safe, and production hardening is applied on the platform, container, or serverless package.
reporting.Why: Leftover defaults and debug functionality are easy targets and can leak sensitive data or provide unintended access.

tests.name: File Extensions Handling for Sensitive Information

reporting.What: Tests how the server handles requests for files with sensitive or risky extensions (such as .bak, .inc, .config) and whether their contents are served or executed.
reporting.Why: Misconfigured extension handling can reveal source code, credentials, or configuration data directly to anyone who requests the file.

tests.name: Review Old Backup and Unreferenced Files for Sensitive Information

reporting.What: Searches for old, backup, and unreferenced files, including leftover cloud storage objects, and verifies that rules blocking access to them cannot be bypassed.
reporting.Why: Forgotten files often contain source code, credentials, or data that the live application was never intended to expose.

tests.name: Enumerate Infrastructure and Application Admin Interfaces

reporting.What: Discovers hidden administrative interfaces, including cloud, orchestration, API-management, and CI/CD consoles, and checks them for weak credentials and excessive exposure.
reporting.Why: Admin interfaces grant high privileges, so any that are discoverable, weakly protected, or reachable by the wrong audience are a direct route to full compromise.

reporting.What: Enumerates which HTTP methods the server supports and tests for access control bypass and method-override techniques.
reporting.Why: Unexpected methods like PUT or DELETE, or overrides that evade restrictions, can allow unauthorized changes or bypass security controls.

reporting.What: Reviews the HSTS header, its directives, preload status, and consistency across the domain and subdomains.
reporting.Why: Without a correct HSTS policy, users can be downgraded to unencrypted HTTP and have their traffic intercepted.

reporting.What: Reviews file permissions on hosts, container images, cloud storage objects, and Kubernetes mounts, and checks how secrets are stored and who can read them.
reporting.Why: Overly broad permissions let attackers or low-privileged users read secrets or modify files, enabling data theft or privilege escalation.

reporting.What: Identifies dangling DNS records pointing to unclaimed external services and assesses whether the parent application trusts the affected subdomain through cookies, CORS, OAuth, or CSP.
reporting.Why: An attacker who claims an abandoned subdomain can serve malicious content from a trusted domain and abuse any trust the main application extends to it.

reporting.What: Assesses access control on cloud storage buckets and containers, the scoping of presigned URLs, and whether versioning or lifecycle settings retain old sensitive data.
reporting.Why: Misconfigured storage is a common cause of large data breaches because exposed objects can be read or modified by anyone.

reporting.What: Reviews the Content-Security-Policy header or meta element for misconfigurations such as overly permissive sources or unsafe directives.
reporting.Why: A weak CSP fails to limit the impact of injection flaws like XSS, removing an important layer of defense.

reporting.What: Checks whether the application, proxy, cache, CDN, and WAF interpret and normalize URL paths consistently, including trailing slashes, case, and encoding.
reporting.Why: Inconsistent path handling can let attackers bypass access rules or poison caches by making one component treat a request differently than another.

reporting.What: Identifies missing or incorrectly configured security headers such as X-Content-Type-Options, Referrer-Policy, and Permissions-Policy, and assesses their impact.
reporting.Why: These headers provide inexpensive browser-enforced protections, and misconfiguration leaves users exposed to attacks the headers are meant to prevent.

reporting.What: Tests whether feature flags and kill-switches that govern security functionality can be manipulated by clients, are enforced server-side, behave safely on failure, and avoid exposing sensitive data or stale code paths.
reporting.Why: If flag state can be tampered with or security checks depend on it, attackers can switch off protections or reach deprecated, unpatched functionality.

reporting.What: Identifies and documents the roles in the application, attempts to switch to or access other roles, and reviews whether permissions are appropriately granular.
reporting.Why: Poorly defined or overly broad roles lead to users holding more access than needed and make privilege escalation easier.

reporting.What: Verifies that registration identity requirements match business and security needs and that the process cannot be abused.
reporting.Why: A weak registration process allows fake, duplicate, or unauthorized accounts that can be used for fraud or to gain unintended access.

reporting.What: Verifies which accounts are allowed to create other accounts and of what type or privilege level.
reporting.Why: If low-privileged users can provision accounts or elevated roles, attackers can create their own privileged access.

tests.name: Account Enumeration and Guessable User Account

reporting.What: Examines registration, login, and reset flows to see whether differences in responses reveal which usernames or accounts exist.
reporting.Why: Confirming valid accounts narrows the target list for brute-force, credential stuffing, and phishing attacks.

reporting.What: Evaluates whether usernames follow a predictable structure or whether the application enforces any username rules.
reporting.Why: Guessable or poorly controlled usernames make enumeration and targeted attacks easier and can enable impersonation.

tests.name: Credentials Transported over an Encrypted Channel

reporting.What: Verifies that login credentials and authentication data are only sent over encrypted channels such as HTTPS.
reporting.Why: Credentials sent in cleartext can be intercepted by anyone on the network path, leading directly to account takeover.

reporting.What: Checks whether the application or its components ship with default accounts and passwords, and whether new accounts get weak or predictable passwords.
reporting.Why: Default credentials are publicly documented and are among the first things attackers try, giving trivial access.

reporting.What: Evaluates whether account lockout or throttling stops brute-force guessing and whether the unlock process can be abused.
reporting.Why: Without effective lockout, attackers can guess passwords at scale, and a flawed unlock process can enable takeover or denial of service.

reporting.What: Tests whether authentication is consistently required on every service and page that should be protected, including via direct requests and parameter tampering.
reporting.Why: A single unprotected path can give attackers full access without needing valid credentials.

reporting.What: Assesses how remember-me and saved-login features generate and store tokens or credentials.
reporting.Why: Insecurely implemented persistence can let attackers steal or forge long-lived sessions and gain lasting access to accounts.

reporting.What: Checks whether sensitive pages or data are cached by the browser and whether they can be viewed after logout using the back button or cache.
reporting.Why: Cached sensitive content can be read by the next person using the device, exposing user data without any authentication.

reporting.What: Evaluates password policy strength, including length, complexity, reuse, and aging requirements, and resistance to dictionary-based guessing.
reporting.Why: Weak password rules make accounts easy to compromise through guessing or credential stuffing.

reporting.What: Assesses how guessable security questions are and whether their answers can be researched or brute-forced.
reporting.Why: Answers are often public or easy to guess, giving attackers a way around the password through account recovery.

tests.name: Weak Password Change or Reset Functionalities

reporting.What: Tests the password change and reset flows for weaknesses like predictable tokens, missing verification, or leakage of reset links.
reporting.Why: Reset functionality is a common takeover route, so flaws let attackers compromise accounts without knowing the password.

reporting.What: Identifies alternative ways to authenticate, such as mobile apps, APIs, or phone support, and tests whether they have weaker protections than the main site.
reporting.Why: Attackers will choose the weakest channel, so a less-protected alternative undermines the strength of the primary login.

reporting.What: Identifies the MFA type in use, evaluates the strength of its implementation, and attempts to bypass it.
reporting.Why: MFA is meant to protect accounts even when passwords are stolen, so any bypass or weakness removes that safeguard.

reporting.What: Tests inputs that reference files or paths to see whether an attacker can read or include files outside the intended directory, and whether filters can be bypassed.
reporting.Why: Path traversal can expose configuration files, credentials, and source code, and may lead to code execution through file inclusion.

reporting.What: Assesses whether unauthenticated users, or users of the same or lower privilege, can reach resources and functions reserved for others.
reporting.Why: Broken access control lets attackers view or change data and functions they should never reach.

reporting.What: Looks for inputs that control privileges or roles and attempts to manipulate them to gain higher access.
reporting.Why: Successful escalation turns a low-privileged account into an administrative one, greatly increasing the impact of any compromise.

reporting.What: Identifies places where objects are referenced by identifiers and tests whether changing them gives access to other users' data.
reporting.Why: IDOR flaws allow attackers to read or modify other users' records simply by altering an ID, often at large scale.

reporting.What: Tests the OAuth 2.0 implementation for known flaws and for use of deprecated or custom flows.
reporting.Why: OAuth mistakes can lead to stolen tokens, account takeover, or unauthorized access to user data via third-party integrations.

reporting.What: Collects and analyzes session tokens for randomness and tamper resistance, and checks whether unsigned cookies carry modifiable data.
reporting.Why: Predictable or modifiable tokens allow attackers to forge sessions and impersonate other users.

reporting.What: Checks that cookies carry proper security attributes such as Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite, Domain, Path, and expiry.
reporting.Why: Missing attributes make cookies easier to steal through XSS or network interception and easier to abuse in cross-site attacks.

reporting.What: Analyzes the login flow to see whether the application issues a new session identifier on authentication or accepts one supplied by an attacker.
reporting.Why: If an attacker can set a victim's session ID before login, they can use it afterward to take over the authenticated session.

reporting.What: Examines how session identifiers and related data are transmitted, cached, and protected through encryption and secure methods.
reporting.Why: Exposed session data in URLs, logs, caches, or cleartext traffic can be harvested and reused to hijack sessions.

reporting.What: Tests whether state-changing requests can be triggered on a logged-in user's behalf from another site without their knowledge.
reporting.Why: CSRF lets attackers make victims perform unwanted actions like changing settings or transferring funds using their own authenticated session.

reporting.What: Assesses the logout interface and verifies the session is properly invalidated on the server after logout.
reporting.Why: If sessions remain valid after logout, stolen or shared-device sessions can still be used by someone else.

reporting.What: Validates that sessions expire after a defined period, including a hard maximum lifetime.
reporting.Why: Long-lived sessions widen the window in which a stolen token or an unattended device can be abused.

reporting.What: Identifies all session variables and tests whether the logical flow that sets them can be broken or manipulated, for example via reused variables across flows.
reporting.Why: Flaws in how session state is built can let attackers bypass authentication or authorization checks without stealing a token.

reporting.What: Identifies session cookies that are vulnerable to capture and attempts to hijack them to assess the risk.
reporting.Why: A hijacked session gives an attacker the full access of the legitimate user without needing their credentials.

reporting.What: Examines JWTs for sensitive data exposure and tests whether they can be tampered with, such as through weak signing or algorithm confusion.
reporting.Why: Forgeable or leaky tokens allow attackers to impersonate users or escalate privileges and may reveal data meant to stay private.

reporting.What: Evaluates how the application handles multiple simultaneous active sessions for a single account.
reporting.Why: Unrestricted concurrent sessions can hide account misuse or credential sharing and make it harder to detect or terminate a compromised session.

reporting.What: Identifies input that is reflected in responses and tests whether it is accepted without proper output encoding, allowing script execution in the victim's browser.
reporting.Why: Reflected XSS can be used to steal sessions, perform actions as the victim, or deliver malicious content through crafted links.

reporting.What: Finds stored user input that is later rendered to other users and tests whether it is properly encoded.
reporting.Why: Stored XSS executes automatically for every viewer, so it can compromise many users, including administrators, without any interaction beyond visiting the page.

reporting.What: Sends requests with unexpected or alternative HTTP verbs to see whether access controls or filters are applied inconsistently.
reporting.Why: Controls that only cover certain methods can be bypassed simply by switching the verb.

reporting.What: Tests how the backend handles duplicate parameters with the same name and whether this can be used to bypass input filters or change behavior.
reporting.Why: Different components may interpret repeated parameters differently, letting attackers smuggle values past validation or alter application logic.

reporting.What: Identifies inputs that reach database queries unsafely and assesses what data or access an attacker could obtain through them.
reporting.Why: SQL injection can lead to theft or modification of the entire database and sometimes full server compromise.

reporting.What: Tests inputs used in LDAP queries for injection that could alter the query's logic.
reporting.Why: A successful attack can bypass authentication or expose directory data such as users and credentials.

reporting.What: Identifies where user input is placed into XML and tests for injection and related attacks such as external entity processing.
reporting.Why: XML injection can alter application logic, expose local files, or trigger server-side requests depending on the parser configuration.

reporting.What: Tests whether user input can inject Server-Side Include directives that the web server will execute.
reporting.Why: SSI injection can disclose files and may allow command execution on the server.

reporting.What: Tests inputs that are used to build XPath queries against XML data for injection.
reporting.Why: XPath injection can bypass authentication or extract data from XML stores, often without any access control on the data.

reporting.What: Tests mail-related features for injection of IMAP or SMTP commands through user-supplied fields.
reporting.Why: Attackers can abuse mail functionality to send spam or phishing from trusted servers or to access mailbox data.

reporting.What: Identifies inputs that are evaluated or included as code by the application and assesses the severity.
reporting.Why: Code injection can give an attacker arbitrary code execution within the application, usually leading to full compromise.

reporting.What: Tests inputs passed to operating system commands for injection and whether special-character or command filters can be bypassed.
reporting.Why: Command injection lets attackers run OS commands on the server, which commonly results in complete system takeover.

reporting.What: Injects format string specifiers into user-controlled fields to see whether they cause unexpected behavior.
reporting.Why: Format string flaws can crash the application, leak memory contents, or in some cases enable code execution.

reporting.What: Finds injections that are stored and only trigger later when another process or user recalls the stored data, and sets up listeners or triggers for that recall.
reporting.Why: These delayed attacks are easy to miss during normal testing but can affect other users or back-end systems once activated.

reporting.What: Tests whether user input reflected into response headers allows injection of CR and LF characters to alter the response.
reporting.Why: Successful splitting can enable cache poisoning, cross-site scripting, and other client-side attacks.

reporting.What: Looks for inconsistencies in how frontend and backend components determine request boundaries, including CL/TE desync and HTTP/2 downgrade issues.
reporting.Why: Smuggling lets attackers bypass front-end security controls, hijack other users' requests, and poison backend queues.

reporting.What: Tests whether the application trusts and dynamically uses the Host header, and whether controls relying on it can be bypassed.
reporting.Why: Abuse of the Host header can enable password reset poisoning, cache poisoning, and access to internal virtual hosts.

reporting.What: Detects points where user input is processed by a server-side template engine, identifies the engine, and assesses exploitability.
reporting.Why: SSTI often leads to remote code execution on the server.

reporting.What: Identifies features that make server-side requests to user-supplied destinations and tests whether they can be directed to internal or unintended targets.
reporting.Why: SSRF can expose internal services and cloud metadata credentials that are otherwise unreachable from outside.

reporting.What: Identifies requests that update objects and tests whether extra fields, such as role or price, can be set that were never meant to be client-modifiable.
reporting.Why: Mass assignment can allow privilege escalation or tampering with protected data by simply adding unexpected fields to a request.

reporting.What: Tests spreadsheet and CSV export features to see whether untrusted values are interpreted as formulas when opened in spreadsheet software, and whether mitigations hold.
reporting.Why: Malicious formulas can exfiltrate data or run commands on the machine of whoever opens the export, such as an administrator.

reporting.What: Identifies code that merges or clones user-controlled properties and tests whether input can modify Object.prototype and reach exploitable gadgets.
reporting.Why: Polluting the prototype can change application behavior globally, leading to XSS, authorization bypass, or remote code execution.

reporting.What: Finds entry points that accept serialized objects from untrusted sources, determines the format, and tests whether manipulated data causes unsafe behavior.
reporting.Why: Unsafe deserialization can allow attackers to tamper with application state or achieve remote code execution.

reporting.What: Triggers errors and analyzes the output returned to see whether it reveals internal details or behaves inconsistently.
reporting.Why: Verbose or inconsistent errors leak information about the technology and logic that helps attackers refine their attacks.

reporting.What: Checks whether the application exposes stack traces or debug output to users when failures occur.
reporting.Why: Stack traces reveal file paths, framework versions, and code structure that significantly aid targeted exploitation.

reporting.What: Reviews TLS configuration, protocol versions, cipher suites, and certificate strength and validity, and checks that TLS cannot be bypassed.
reporting.Why: Weak or misconfigured TLS allows traffic to be intercepted or downgraded, exposing sensitive data in transit.

reporting.What: Identifies encrypted messages that use padding and tests whether error responses reveal enough to decrypt or forge them.
reporting.Why: A padding oracle can let attackers decrypt protected data or craft valid encrypted values without knowing the key.

tests.name: Sensitive Information Sent via Unencrypted Channels

reporting.What: Identifies sensitive data transmitted over any channel and assesses whether those channels are encrypted and private.
reporting.Why: Data sent in cleartext through any channel can be captured and read by anyone able to observe the traffic.

reporting.What: Identifies the use of weak, outdated, or incorrectly implemented encryption and hashing algorithms.
reporting.Why: Broken primitives can be reversed or brute-forced, undermining the confidentiality and integrity of passwords and data.

reporting.What: Tests whether data checks are enforced on the server, including type, range, allowed values, and relationships that the frontend restricts.
reporting.Why: Client-side validation is easily bypassed, so missing server-side checks let attackers submit invalid data that breaks business rules.

reporting.What: Looks for guessable, predictable, or hidden fields and functionality and submits logically valid data to bypass the normal workflow.
reporting.Why: Forged requests can skip intended steps or trigger functions the interface does not expose, enabling abuse of business processes.

reporting.What: Reviews components that move, store, or handle data and attempts to insert, change, or delete values that should be disallowed by the business logic.
reporting.Why: Weak integrity controls allow unauthorized tampering with data, leading to fraud, corruption, or incorrect system behavior.

reporting.What: Examines functionality that is affected by timing and develops misuse cases, such as race conditions or time-based information leaks.
reporting.Why: Timing weaknesses can reveal information or allow actions to be repeated or reordered in ways that break business rules.

tests.name: Number of Times a Function Can Be Used Limits

reporting.What: Identifies functions that should be limited in how often they can be used, such as coupons or votes, and checks the limits are enforced.
reporting.Why: Missing or bypassable limits allow abuse like repeated redemptions, resource exhaustion, or financial loss.

reporting.What: Attempts to skip steps or perform them out of order in multi-step processes and checks whether the application enforces the intended sequence.
reporting.Why: Users who bypass required steps, such as payment or approval, can obtain goods or access they were not entitled to.

reporting.What: Reviews results of earlier tests to see how the application reacts to aggressive input and whether its detection and response defenses are adequate.
reporting.Why: Without effective monitoring and response to attacks, malicious activity goes unnoticed and attackers can probe freely.

reporting.What: Tests whether file types that the system should reject are properly blocked and handled safely, including via batch uploads.
reporting.Why: Accepting unexpected file types can lead to stored malicious content, resource abuse, or processing errors.

reporting.What: Attempts to upload potentially dangerous files, such as web shells or malware-bearing documents, and determines whether they are accepted and processed.
reporting.Why: Malicious uploads can lead to code execution on the server or attacks against other users who download the files.

reporting.What: Examines how the payment flow works and tests its logic and security, including price, quantity, and transaction manipulation.
reporting.Why: Flaws in payment logic lead directly to financial loss and fraud, and may expose cardholder data.

reporting.What: Identifies DOM sinks in client-side code and builds payloads for each sink type to see whether attacker-controlled data reaches them.
reporting.Why: DOM XSS happens entirely in the browser, can evade server-side defenses, and allows script execution in the victim's session.

reporting.What: Identifies sinks and injection points where user-controlled data can be executed as JavaScript in the browser.
reporting.Why: Arbitrary script execution allows theft of data and sessions and actions performed on behalf of the user.

reporting.What: Finds points where user input is rendered as HTML and assesses the severity of content that can be injected.
reporting.Why: Injected HTML can be used for phishing, fake login forms, or defacement within a trusted site.

reporting.What: Identifies inputs that control client-side redirects or URL handling and assesses where users can be sent.
reporting.Why: Open redirects let attackers send victims to malicious sites from a trusted domain, supporting phishing and token theft.

reporting.What: Identifies places where user input is placed into stylesheets and assesses the impact of injected CSS.
reporting.Why: Injected CSS can alter the page to deceive users or extract sensitive page data through style-based techniques.

reporting.What: Finds client-side code that builds resource paths from user input, such as script, frame, or request sources, with weak validation.
reporting.Why: Attackers can make the page load or request attacker-chosen resources, leading to script injection or unintended requests.

reporting.What: Identifies endpoints implementing CORS and tests whether the policy allows untrusted origins to read responses, especially with credentials.
reporting.Why: A permissive CORS policy lets malicious sites read sensitive data from the application using a victim's browser.

reporting.What: Tests whether the application can be embedded in a frame on another site so users can be tricked into clicking hidden elements.
reporting.Why: Clickjacking can trick users into performing sensitive actions without realizing it.

reporting.What: Identifies WebSocket use and applies the same tests as for normal HTTP, such as origin checks, authentication, authorization, and input validation.
reporting.Why: WebSockets often lack the protections applied to regular requests, leaving a real-time channel open to hijacking and injection.

reporting.What: Assesses the use of postMessage and similar APIs, checking that message origins are verified and received data is validated and handled safely.
reporting.Why: Unchecked messages from other windows can inject data or script, or leak sensitive information to untrusted origins.

reporting.What: Checks whether sensitive data is stored in localStorage, sessionStorage, or similar, and reviews how stored values are used for injection risks.
reporting.Why: Data in browser storage is readable by any script on the page, so XSS or local access can expose tokens and personal information.

reporting.What: Locates sensitive data delivered in script-like responses and tests whether another site can include and read it.
reporting.Why: XSSI can leak private data to attacker-controlled sites through the victim's authenticated browser.

reporting.What: Checks whether links that open new tabs or windows expose the original page to the opened page through window.opener.
reporting.Why: A malicious linked page could redirect the original tab to a phishing page, deceiving users who return to it.

reporting.What: Identifies the client-side framework and tests whether user input reflected into the DOM is evaluated by the template engine, enabling script execution.
reporting.Why: Template syntax injection can give attackers XSS even where normal HTML encoding is in place.

reporting.What: Discovers all API endpoints and parameters, documented or not, including those revealed in client-side HTML and JavaScript.
reporting.Why: Undocumented endpoints and parameters are often less protected and cannot be tested unless they are found.

reporting.What: Tests whether the API verifies, for every object request, that the caller is authorized to access that specific object.
reporting.Why: Missing object-level checks let users read or modify other users' data and are among the most common and damaging API flaws.

reporting.What: Identifies API responses that return more data than the client needs, such as hashes, tokens, PII, or internal details, relying on the client to filter it.
reporting.Why: Anyone can read raw API responses, so over-shared fields leak sensitive data regardless of what the interface displays.

reporting.What: Tests whether the API restricts privileged functions, such as admin operations, to users with the right role or privilege.
reporting.Why: Without function-level checks, ordinary users can call administrative endpoints and perform actions beyond their rights.

reporting.What: Assesses GraphQL deployments for production-ready configuration, input validation against common attacks, and proper access controls.
reporting.Why: GraphQL features like introspection, deep queries, and flexible fields can expose schema details, enable denial of service, and bypass authorization when misconfigured.

reporting.What: Finds all WebAssembly modules the application loads, identifies the toolchain and source language, and looks for debug artifacts and embedded URLs, endpoints, or hostnames.
reporting.Why: Wasm modules can hide logic and secrets or expose debug information and infrastructure details, and they must be located before they can be assessed.
